surveys.lens_summary:
STATE OF THE ART, 2025 to Oct 2026 (representation geometry and causal abstraction)

1) The linear representation hypothesis (LRH) is now known to be partial. Its formal statements (Park et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03658 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01506) and SAE dictionaries treat a feature as a direction. Several results break that picture:
- Engels et al. found circular day and month features and showed they are causal (https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14860).
- Kantamneni and Tegmark found numbers on a helix used for addition (https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00873).
- Csordás et al. found GRUs that encode position by magnitude (an "onion" code) rather than by direction (https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.10920).
- Anthropic's line-breaking paper is the most important recent example (Gurnee et al., Oct 2025 / Jan 2026; https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/linebreaks/index.html , https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.04480). Character counts lie on curved 1-D manifolds. Attention QK matrices "twist" (rotate) one manifold against another, and the final decision comes from arranging the estimates so that a linear boundary separates them. The authors name a "complexity tax": dictionary features break the manifold into many small pieces and interactions. They also say their manifold search was "an existence proof more than a general recipe" and call for "unsupervised discovery of other kinds of geometric structures."
- Open-model replications show the counting helix in Pythia-410m, Qwen3 and Gemma (T-Tech, https://t-tech-manifolds.hf.space/).

2) Discovering feature manifolds has become a busy subfield in 2026, but all of it works at a single layer, and none of it learns how computation moves between manifolds.
- Theory: Modell et al. model features as metric spaces (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18235). Karkada et al. explain the geometry as a consequence of translation symmetry in co-occurrence statistics (https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15029). Michaud et al. model how SAE scaling behaves when features are manifolds (https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02565).
- How SAEs handle manifolds: Bhalla, Fel, Geiger, Lubana et al. show that SAEs "dilute" a manifold into fragmented local detectors, and recover manifolds post hoc with an Ising-style grouping of atoms (https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.28119). Gerasimov et al. find that individual SAE features change across random seeds while the subspaces they span are reproducible (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12138).
- New architectures and fitting methods: SMIXAE, a sparse mixture of autoencoders (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09224); supervised MDS (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01025); NLMCD with a concept-based alignment score across layers and models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01821, 1 Oct 2026).
- Interventions: manifold steering, which moves activations along geodesics of a fitted manifold (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05115). MAxBench finds that affine subspaces, mainly through their offsets, beat rank-1 directions, and that no method consistently beats prompting (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13072).
- An important caveat: "When Models Don't Manipulate Manifolds" (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37680) finds that Qwen2.5-7B represents numbers on curved geometry but reads them out through a linear direction when comparing them. The geometry you can observe is not always the geometry the model uses.

3) Computational primitives beyond linear features exist but are not built on manifolds.
- Cross-layer transcoders (CLTs) and attribution graphs (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/methods.html). The QK feature-interaction work (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attention-qk/index.html).
- Sparse mixtures of linear transforms (MOLT, https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/bulk-update/index.html). Its intuition section already pictures a rank-2 "+3" rotation acting on digits arranged on a circle.
- Mixture of Decoders (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21364), Jacobian SAEs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18147) and the Local Interaction Basis (https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10928).
- None of these has explicit manifold-valued variables, typed transformations between them, or a measurement of the complexity tax.

4) Causal abstraction is in a foundational crisis.
- Background: DAS (https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.02536), the JMLR theory of causal abstraction (https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04709), and subspace-patching illusions (https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17030).
- Sutter et al. (NeurIPS 2025 spotlight, https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08802) prove that with unconstrained non-linear alignment maps, any network can be mapped to any algorithm. Randomly initialised LMs reach 100% interchange-intervention accuracy (IIA) on IOI, and they state there is "no principled way" to balance map complexity against accuracy.
- Responses so far are partial: unsupervised discovery of low-rank causal abstractions (Saulus et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19594), per-input bucketing (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02234), and evidence that correct causal variables predict out-of-distribution behaviour (Huang et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11770).
- MDL and Pareto probing (https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.12298 , https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02180) solved the same problem for correlational probes, not for interventions.

5) Superposition theory has little direct confirmation in real models.
- Theory: Toy Models of Superposition (https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10652) and mathematical models of computation in superposition (https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05451). Liu et al. link superposition to scaling laws (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10465).
- The toy "compressed computation" model is disputed (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14673).
- Real-model evidence: Janiak et al. find stable regions in the residual stream (https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.17113). Ferreira da Silva and Heimersheim (June 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24964) find feature-specific error correction in six LLMs: the response exponent is p>2 along candidate feature directions. They also report that maximizing p alone finds directions that do not otherwise behave like features.
- Anthropic's interference-weights work (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2026/interference_effectiveness_helpfulness/index.html) and its J-space work, which uses a first-order Jacobian lens (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2026/workspace/index.html).
- Apollo's critique "Activation space interpretability may be doomed" (https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/gYfpPbww3wQRaxAFD) argues that decompositions of activation statistics find features of the data rather than features the model computes with.

WHAT IS MISSING
(a) A circuit-tracing instrument whose units are manifold-valued variables and whose edges are low-complexity geometric maps, learned without supervision across layers. This is the step after SAEs and attribution graphs that Anthropic explicitly asks for.
(b) A complexity-calibrated, null-tested criterion that makes non-linear causal abstraction non-vacuous and states each variable's encoding format.
(c) A criterion grounded in the model's own computation, not in activation statistics, for which directions and manifolds are real features, plus a direct measurement of superposition capacity in real LMs.

The three proposals below give one instrument for each gap. They share one currency, description length in bits, and one standard: a claim is validated by intervention against a null. They can plug into interp-lab's evidence grading, its planted-ground-truth calibration and its placebo controls.

proposals.title: GeoTrace: geometric replacement models and manifold attribution graphs
proposals.gap: All current circuit-tracing primitives (SAEs, transcoders, CLTs, MOLT, MxD, JSAE) use 1-D linear features or linear transforms of the whole activation as units. When the model computes on a manifold, these units break it into many local pieces. Anthropic calls this the 'complexity tax': their line-breaking analysis needed weeks of manual, supervised manifold fitting. They state that their search was 'an existence proof more than a general recipe' and call for methods that 'extend the dictionary learning paradigm to unsupervised discovery of other kinds of geometric structures' and 'automatically surface simpler structures' (https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.04480). The 2026 manifold methods do not fill this gap. SMIXAE, Bhalla/Fel et al.'s grouping, NLMCD, SMDS and manifold steering each find or use a manifold at one site. None learns how one manifold is transformed into another, for example that an attention head rotates a count manifold by an offset, or that an MLP adds angles. So there is no circuit-level tool that expresses computation as geometry, and no measurement of how much of a model's computation is geometric versus lookup-table-like. The comparison-task paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37680) shows the question is real: observed curvature can be ignored by a linear readout. Only a tool that models edges as functions can separate geometry that is used from geometry that is merely present.
proposals.why_new_understanding:
GeoTrace changes the unit of mechanistic explanation from 'which features fire and connect' to 'which variables, of which shape, are transformed by which operations'. This is the level at which Anthropic's best manual result was stated, and it would now be available unsupervised and at scale.

It answers questions no current tool can measure:
- How much of an LM's computation is geometric versus lookup-table-like, by layer, task and model size?
- Is there a small reusable 'instruction set' of geometric operations? The QK twist, translation by token increment, and orthogonal arrangement for a linear readout are candidates. Do these motifs recur across counting, position, dates, numbers and syntax, and across model families? That would be a universality claim at the level of operations.
- When curvature exists, is it read (edges depend on angle or curvature) or ignored (edges are linear projections), as in the comparison task? This would settle the 'observed vs used geometry' question.

Because edges are explicit functions, the model makes quantitative predictions for novel inputs. That makes it falsifiable in a way current feature graphs are not. Automatically generating 'visual illusions', which Anthropic did by hand, becomes a routine test.

proposals.minimal_demo:
Stage 1, ground-truth toys (CPU):
(a) A 1-layer transformer on modular addition mod 113 (Nanda et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.05217). Success:
- GeoTrace recovers exactly the key Fourier frequencies, as found by DFT, as S^1 units;
- it labels the MLP edge as angle addition with R^2 > 0.95;
- the full graph keeps ≥95% of accuracy and logit difference using ≤3× (#key frequencies) units;
- a matched transcoder needs ≥10× more bits for the same fidelity. This tests the lookup-table versus rotation claim from the MOLT note.
(b) A 2–4-layer transformer trained on synthetic fixed-width wrapped text. Success: it recovers the count manifold, the twist in the boundary-head QK with offset δ within ±1 character, and the linear newline decision.

Stage 2, real models (one GPU):
- Line breaking at width W in Pythia-410m or Qwen3-1.7B, which T-Tech showed perform the task; Gemma-2-2b if its behaviour checks out, since it has Gemma Scope and circuit-tracer CLTs.
- The greater-than task in GPT-2 small (Hanna et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.00586), using the released GPT-2 transcoders. This is a genuinely open test of whether the late-MLP greater-than computation is a threshold on a 1-D year coordinate.
Pre-registered metrics:
(i) Complexity-tax ratio: bits for the CLT graph divided by bits for the GeoTrace graph at matched replacement faithfulness (KL on task tokens). Success: ≥5× on manifold tasks and about 1× on a non-geometric control task such as IOI. Parity on the control shows the method is not cheating.
(ii) Geodesic patching of the count coordinate. Success: the predicted and observed change in P(newline) correlate with Spearman ρ > 0.8, and IIA beats rank-matched linear DAS with lower off-target KL.
(iii) Automatically generated illusions, the decisive test. From the fitted edge functions, synthesize input edits predicted to shift a coordinate, for example tokens whose learned length increment is mis-estimated, or distractors that capture a twist head. Pre-register the direction and size of each effect. Success: ≥75% of predicted effects are significant in the predicted direction, against ≤10% for matched control edits.

Stage 3, discovery: a catalog of units and edge-motif frequencies across GPT-2 small, Pythia-410m and Gemma-2-2b, plus a cross-model test of whether the twist and translation motifs recur.
proposals.compute_needs: Toys: a few CPU-hours. Real models: one 24GB GPU. Caching 20–50M tokens of activations for Pythia-410m or GPT-2 small takes about 2–6 GPU-hours. Grouping and chart fitting on existing dictionaries is mostly CPU. Training the geometric transcoders and running the interventional-consistency loss takes roughly 10–40 GPU-hours per model. Gemma-2-2b is feasible on 24GB with cached activations. The method scales because it is built on dictionaries that already exist at frontier scale: grouping and edge fitting cost the same order as CLT training.
proposals.risks:
- The choice of manifold topology may be unstable or unidentifiable, since many curves fit noisy data. Mitigations: MDL selection, a persistent-homology prior, and cross-seed reproducibility checks (cf. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12138).
- Most computation in small models may not be geometric, so GeoTrace degrades to a CLT. The 'geometric fraction' is still a reportable, falsifiable result.
- Comparing bits across different model classes is subtle. Mitigation: use prequential codes and report full Pareto curves, not single points.
- Attention edges with several interacting manifolds may be hard to fit. Start with single-manifold QK kernels.
- Small open models may lack rich behaviours such as line breaking at GPT-2 scale. Verify behaviour first (T-Tech shows Pythia-410m and Qwen3-1.7B can do it).
- Scope creep: build in stages (toy, then one real task, then the catalog).

proposals.title: Occam Causal Abstraction: null-calibrated, description-length causal abstraction with a representation-format ladder
proposals.gap:
Sutter et al. (NeurIPS 2025 spotlight, https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08802) proved that with expressive alignment maps, causal abstraction is vacuous: random-init LMs reach 100% IIA on IOI with RevNet maps. Without the linearity assumption, they say, there is 'no principled way to balance' complexity and accuracy.

The field therefore uses linear DAS by convention. That convention:
- misses or mislabels variables encoded non-linearly (circles, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14860; helices, https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00873; magnitude or 'onion' codes, https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.10920; curved count manifolds, https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.04480);
- remains open to interpretability illusions (https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17030).

No method today decides, with calibrated significance, which format a causally used variable is encoded in. No method makes non-linear causal abstraction non-vacuous. There is also no census of how often the LRH actually holds for causal variables in real LMs.

MDL and Pareto probing (https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.12298 , https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02180) solved the analogous problem for correlational probes only. Saulus et al. 2026 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19594) learn low-rank abstractions but do not price map complexity or select a format. MAxBench (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13072) compares geometries for steering, not for causal abstraction.
proposals.why_new_understanding:
(1) It turns causal abstraction from vacuous back into falsifiable. Every mechanistic claim gets a price in bits and a significance level against random networks. This is a principled answer to the non-linear representation dilemma, not a convention.

(2) It yields the first rigorous LRH census of causally used variables in real LMs. What fraction is linear, affine, circular, magnitude-coded or genuinely higher-complexity once complexity is paid for? Does the fraction change with depth, model size or training (Pythia checkpoints)? The answer changes what interpretability tools should assume. If it is mostly linear or affine, the field's main bet is justified. If a sizable fraction is curved or magnitude-coded, SAE and DAS pipelines are systematically blind to it.

(3) It gives one common currency, bits, for comparing explanations produced by SAE circuits, DAS, GeoTrace or natural-language hypotheses. A shared scale like this is missing today.

proposals.compute_needs: Light. DAS and the other ladder maps are small, and the nulls (random init, permuted H) are cheap. GPT-2 small and Pythia-70m/160m run on CPU or a laptop GPU. The census over about 20 variables × 3 models × 7 ladder rungs × bootstrap is roughly 20–60 GPU-hours on one modest GPU. The DSL algorithm-search extension is the expensive part: budget a further 50–100 GPU-hours, or restrict it to toy tasks.
proposals.risks:
- Codelength estimates depend on block size and optimizer. Mitigations: use several coding schemes and report the agreement between them, and calibrate on planted ground truth.
- The ladder may miss the true format. Report 'none of the ladder' when the RevNet rung wins only marginally over the nulls.
- The census may come back 'almost everything is affine'. That is a valuable and publishable answer.
- The DSL search space can explode. Keep the DSL typed and small, and seed it with known hypotheses.
- Interchange-intervention data are themselves distribution-dependent. Include counterfactual families that are out of distribution.

proposals.title: Error-Correction Spectroscopy: measuring superposition and feature validity from the model's own defenses
proposals.gap:
There is no criterion, independent of any dictionary and grounded in the model's own computation, for which directions or manifolds are real features of a model.
- SAE latents change with the random seed (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12138).
- Activation-statistics decompositions may find structure in the data rather than structure the model uses (https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/gYfpPbww3wQRaxAFD).
- The 'used vs observed geometry' gap is real: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37680 finds curvature that the model ignores.

The core predictions of superposition theory remain almost untested in real LMs: features are stored and computed in superposition with feature-specific error correction and finite capacity (https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10652 , https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05451). The toy-model debate on compressed computation is unresolved (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14673). Ferreira da Silva and Heimersheim (June 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24964) gave the first real-LLM evidence of feature-specific error correction: p>2 superellipse response exponents along candidate directions in six LLMs. They only test directions supplied in advance, though, and they report that maximizing p alone finds non-feature directions. Discovery, capacity measurement and manifold-level tests are therefore all open. Janiak et al.'s stable regions (https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.17113) and Anthropic's first-order Jacobian-lens J-space (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2026/workspace/index.html) do not measure non-quadratic, feature-specific defense or its capacity.
proposals.idea:
A perturbation instrument that reads the model's error-correcting code at any layer. It has four measurements and one learning objective.

(1) PRIVILEGE SCORE. For any candidate unit, measure how the downstream response changes under norm-matched rotations of the activation toward the candidate and toward mixtures of candidates. Candidates can be SAE or transcoder latents, probe or steering vectors, or the tangent and normal directions of GeoTrace units. Compute:
- the superellipse exponent p;
- the width of the plateau-breaking angle;
- the basin-return ratio: the fraction of a perturbation that layers L+1..L+k remove.
The score uses mixed-direction controls, random-direction and PCA controls, and random-init model controls.

(2) CAPACITY CURVE. Superpose k candidate features with random signs at sub-threshold amplitude and measure where error correction collapses as k grows. Fit the curve to superposition-theory predictions for interference scaling (for example, noise growing like sqrt(k/d) for near-random embeddings). This gives empirical estimates of simultaneous-feature capacity and effective features per dimension for each layer, each model size (the Pythia suite) and each training step.

(3) MANIFOLD ATTRACTOR TEST. For a candidate manifold, split perturbations into tangent and normal components. Candidates include Engels's day and month circles, the line-position helix and GeoTrace units. Measure downstream gain along each. The prediction is that a used manifold has its tangent directions preserved, because they carry information, and its normal directions contracted, because the model snaps back to the manifold. The ratio of normal to tangent gain operationalizes 'the model uses this geometry'. It applies equally to the case where curvature is ignored.

(4) STEERING DIAGNOSIS. Test whether failures of linear steering, such as off-manifold drift and the need for large coefficients, are explained by error correction undoing the edit.

(5) PRIVILEGE-ANCHORED DICTIONARY LEARNING. Add a privilege term to the SAE objective, estimated cheaply with JVP or finite-difference probes. Data reconstruction anchors the search, which avoids the reported failure of maximizing p alone. Then test whether privileged atoms are more stable across seeds and more causally important than ordinary SAE atoms.

proposals.compute_needs: The work is forward-pass heavy but embarrassingly parallel. GPT-2 small at about 5k candidates × 30 anchor prompts × 15 angles × a few mixtures is roughly 5–10M partial forward passes, about 2–6 GPU-hours on one modest GPU or around a day on CPU for a subset. Capacity curves across Pythia 70m–1.4b and selected checkpoints take about 20–50 GPU-hours. Privilege-anchored SAE training adds about 10–20 GPU-hours with JVP estimates. The method scales with sampling, because only candidate directions are scored rather than the whole space.
proposals.risks:
- Generic nonlinearities such as LayerNorm, attention softmax and saturation could produce p>2 or plateaus unrelated to features. Random-init, random-direction, PCA and mixture controls are essential, and the known failure of p-maximization must be guarded against.
- Error correction may be weak or noisy in sub-billion models, so the effect sizes may be small. The scaling trend across Pythia is then the key output.
- Capacity-theory predictions depend on assumptions about embedding geometry. Fit families of curves rather than a single law, and validate on toys.
- The choice of downstream response measure (residual L2, logit KL) may change results. Report all of them.
- Heavy dependence on Ferreira da Silva & Heimersheim's protocol. Novelty rests on discovery, capacity, the manifold tangent/normal test and the scaling study, which must be clearly separated from replication.

surveys.lens_summary:
STATE OF THE ART (Oct 2026), lens = training dynamics + weight-based interpretability.

(1) PARAMETER DECOMPOSITION has gone from toy models to a 67M LM. APD (Braun et al., Jan 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.14926) led to SPD (Bushnaq, Braun, Sharkey, Jun 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20790; Goodfire page https://www.goodfire.com/research/stochastic-param-decomp). SPD was extended to transformers and GPT-2-small (Christensen & Riggs, https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08854). The current state of the art is VPD, adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (Goodfire, 5 May 2026, https://www.goodfire.com/research/interpreting-lm-parameters ; AF linkpost https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/eAQZaiC3PcBhS4HjM). It splits 24 matrices of a 4-layer, 67M-parameter model into 38,912 rank-1 subcomponents (about 10k alive), decomposes attention, and compares well against transcoders and CLTs. Its own stated weak points:
- Adversarial robustness collapses after about 20 PGD steps (KL 0.83 at 20 steps, 40.2 at 320).
- Rank-1 subcomponents still need a separate clustering step.
- The loss choices are heuristic, and nonlinear interactions between subcomponents are not characterized.
- Future work it names includes "project parameter gradients onto the subcomponent basis to interpret training and finetuning" and "apply VPD to weight diffs."
- The SPD page says it has only been validated "on models where we know what to look for." Neither identifiability nor seed stability is addressed. By analogy, SAEs share only about 30% of features across seeds (Paulo & Belrose, https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16615).

Related weight-space approaches:
- L3D decomposes per-sample gradients (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.00194).
- Sparse Weight Decomposition factorizes weights into sparse factors (Aug 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03913).
- OpenAI's weight-sparse transformers (ICML 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13653) give interpretable but expensive models, and a replication questions their faithfulness (https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/sHpZZnRDLg7ccX9aF/weight-sparse-circuits-may-be-interpretable-yet-unfaithful).
- Anthropic's interference-weights line (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/interference-weights/index.html ; Aug 2026 https://transformer-circuits.pub/2026/interference_effectiveness_helpfulness/index.html) names noisy global weights as a bottleneck for global circuit analysis.
- The toy-model ground truth is contested: "Compressed computation is (probably) not computation in superposition" (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14673).

(2) SLT / DEVELOPMENTAL INTERPRETABILITY. Timaeus is now Resolution (https://resolution.org/research/). Its methods are the LLC (https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.12108), the rLLC (https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02984), stagewise development (https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02364) and transient structure explained by a loss-versus-complexity tradeoff (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17745). From there the work moved to susceptibilities:
- Structural inference (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18274)
- Embryology (https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.00331)
- Spectroscopy, 510 clusters in Pythia-14M (https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12703)
- Spectroscopy at Pythia-1.4B, about 57k clusters, 4,800 H200-hours (https://timaeus.co/research/2026-04-21-spectroscopy-main)
- Patterning, which reweights data to speed up or suppress induction-head formation and to pick between algorithms, validated by retraining on a 3M-parameter model (https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13548)
- A linear-response primer (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07980)
- Bayesian influence functions (https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26544), the loss kernel (https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26537) and stagewise influence dynamics (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12071)
- LLC tied to compressibility and MDL (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12077)

The key limitation: susceptibility "components" are whole heads or whole MLP layers (410 components for Pythia-1.4B). The authors say "a general circuit-finding method ... has not been published," and SGLD hyperparameters are fragile. Library: https://github.com/timaeus-research/devinterp

(3) TRAINING-TRAJECTORY ANALYSIS. Methods that track features or credit across training:
- POLCA (ICLR 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15872) finds hidden breakthroughs by allocating per-example loss changes onto a Hessian-eigenvector basis. Its authors write that "a non-orthogonal basis might separate [concepts in superposition] more cleanly."
- ExPLAIND (ICML 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20076) treats AdamW training as a kernel machine to get parameter-wise and step-wise influence. A Sep 2026 Pythia study uses it to decompose memorization dynamics (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34933).
- LCA (https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.01440) assigns loss change to individual parameters along the training path.
- Activation-space crosscoders across checkpoints: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05291 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.17196.
- Mechanistic Data Attribution (ICML 2026 oral, https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21996) traces pre-specified heads to their training data with influence functions.

Work on how and when mechanisms form:
- Capability-emergence forecasting from precursor heads (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19000).
- A driven-nucleation "kinetics" rate law (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27281; single author, not peer reviewed).
- Grokking chimera transplants (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06628).
- A warning that update-based spectral analyses are distorted by the AdamW optimizer (https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25143).
- Training-time causal clamping of induction heads (https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07129), and strategy coopetition, where one in-context-learning strategy scaffolds another (https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.05631).

Theories that still lack a mechanism-level test: the Quantization Model of scaling (https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.13506) versus superposition-driven scaling (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10465). Both remain untested where mechanisms live, in the weights.

(4) MODEL DIFFING is crowded on the activation side: BatchTopK crosscoders (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02922), the Activation Difference Lens (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13900), Delta-Crosscoder (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04426) and stage-wise diffing (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/model-diffing/index.html). On the weight side it is thin: DIT (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05092) and WARP (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01686). Parameter decomposition of weight diffs has been proposed but, as far as I found, not done.

WHAT IS UNDER-TOOLED: every parameter-decomposition method works on a single checkpoint, and every developmental method works with coarse units (heads, layers, Hessian eigenvectors) or units chosen in advance. Nobody decomposes the whole training trajectory into mechanisms, so nobody can say from weights alone when each mechanism formed, which data built it, which mechanisms it depended on, or whether the "quanta" picture of learning is mechanistically real. The open-problems review (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16496) explicitly asks for decomposition that takes "a more dynamic, developmental view of how mechanistic structure emerges."

NOTE: my web-search budget ran out before one final novelty check, on whether anyone has applied CP/PARAFAC tensor decomposition to stacks of training checkpoints. Nothing I found does this, but the build agent should re-check early. The tensor-identifiability references I rely on are Kruskal (1977) uniqueness and the generic CP identifiability result of Chiantini, Ottaviani & Vannieuwenhoven (https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.4157).

proposals.title: Chronoscope: Developmental Parameter Decomposition (DPD). Use the training trajectory as the third tensor mode that makes weight-space mechanisms identifiable, then build a mechanism-by-data-by-time ledger of learning.
proposals.gap:
1. Parameter decomposition (APD, SPD, VPD) factorizes one weight matrix per layer at one checkpoint. A matrix factorization is never unique, so these methods depend on heuristic minimality and simplicity priors.
- VPD's adversarial faithfulness collapses after about 20 PGD steps.
- SPD/VPD still need a post-hoc clustering step to group rank-1 subcomponents into mechanisms, and SPD's own page says it was only validated on models 'where we know what to look for.'
- The seed-stability analogue is bad for SAEs: about 30% of features are shared across seeds (Paulo & Belrose 2025).

2. Developmental tools have the opposite problem: the time axis is good, the units are coarse.
- Susceptibility spectroscopy uses whole heads and MLP layers.
- POLCA uses Hessian eigenvectors, and its authors say a non-orthogonal basis might separate superposed concepts better.
- Crosscoders-through-time work in activation space and cannot say which weights implement a change.
- MDA needs units specified in advance.

3. Goodfire lists 'project parameter gradients onto the subcomponent basis to interpret training' and 'apply VPD to weight diffs' as future work, and the 2025 Open Problems review asks for a 'developmental view' of decomposition. No published method recovers, from weights, which mechanisms exist, when each was born or died, and which data built it.
proposals.idea:
Stack log-spaced checkpoints W^l(t_1..t_T) and fit one shared library of rank-1 parameter components, each with its own time course:

W^l(t) = a_l(t)·W^l(0) + Σ_c g_c(t)·u_c v_c^T + E^l(t)

- W(0) is the random-init substrate with a fitted decay a(t), to absorb weight decay.
- u_c v_c^T are shared components in the residual-stream basis, which is fixed within a single run.
- g_c(t) is a growth curve parameterized as a monotone birth spline minus a sparse monotone death spline, so components can appear and disappear.

Stage 1 (data-free, cheap): a sparse CP/PARAFAC fit of the out×in×time tensor of weight changes. A matrix factorization at one checkpoint has rotational freedom. A 3-way CP decomposition is essentially unique under Kruskal-type conditions, and generically identifiable even when overcomplete, up to ranks that grow with d_out·d_in·T/(d_out+d_in+T). Mechanisms that overlap in the final weights but grew on different schedules therefore become separable.

Stage 2 (mechanistic refinement): SPD/VPD-style training. For each batch:
- Sample a checkpoint t.
- Compute causal importances CI_c(x,t) with a shared CI network conditioned on t.
- Run the masked model at checkpoint t and penalize KL to the true checkpoint output, plus weight faithfulness, plus input-sparsity of CI, plus total variation of g_c over log-time. VPD-style adversarial masks are optional.
- Optionally add an L3D-style term that makes per-example gradients sparse in the component basis.
- Subcomponents with matching growth curves are clustered into mechanisms. Shared birth time is a clustering signal that SPD/VPD lack.

Stage 3 (ledger): integrate the loss change between checkpoints along the component coordinates, LCA-style with Runge-Kutta: ΔL(x) ≈ Σ_c ∫ ∂L(x)/∂g_c dg_c + residual. This gives an exact accounting of each token's learning by (mechanism × data cluster × time window). Clustering tokens by their ledger profiles is POLCA with a mechanistic basis.

Deliverables in the open-source repo (interp-big):
- `chronoscope` library: checkpoint IO for HF Pythia revisions plus a log-spaced checkpointing trainer, built on Goodfire's MIT-licensed param-decomp nano reference.
- A planted-mechanism toy suite with ground truth.
- A pre-registered evaluation harness.
- An atlas viewer. Each component card shows its input profile, growth curve, birth/death time, ledger share, and downstream links via virtual weights.
- Export of components as feature records to interp-lab for causal grading.
- The same machinery applied to a base→finetune trajectory gives mechanism-resolved model diffing: which components are new, amplified, or suppressed, and which finetuning data built each.
proposals.why_new_understanding:
1. Identifiability. It addresses a foundational weakness of weight-based interpretability: decompositions are not unique. The proposal turns that into a testable claim, that training history makes mechanisms identifiable. If true, parameter decomposition stops being 'one useful basis' and becomes a recoverable fact about the network.

2. Questions no current instrument can answer:
- Is learning quantized at the mechanism level, with discrete sigmoid 'births', as the Quantization Model claims? Or does everything co-grow continuously, as superposition-scaling theory suggests? This adjudicates between two live theories of neural scaling, directly in weights.
- Do transient 'fossil' mechanisms exist that are built and then dismantled? They are invisible to any method that only reads the final checkpoint.
- Which data built which mechanism, discovered without supervision rather than for units chosen in advance?
- Do mechanisms split and merge over training, a developmental version of feature splitting?

3. Every claim is checkable against ground truth (planted toy models, the known grokking story) and against held-out per-token loss trajectories, so the atlas is falsifiable rather than a picture.

proposals.minimal_demo:
D1. Identifiability phase diagram, with ground truth.
- Setup (a): the TMS and ResidualMLP toys from goodfire-ai/param-decomp, with log-uniform feature frequencies so features are learned at different times.
- Setup (b): a 2-layer transformer trained on a mixture of 8–16 synthetic tasks with known circuits: bigram tables, skip-trigrams, induction/copy, small lookups.
- Sweep the superposition ratio (features/dims from 1 to 8) and the spread of onset times.
- Metrics: mean max cosine similarity (MMCS) to ground-truth mechanism weights; seed stability (fraction of components matched at cos > 0.9 across 5 decomposition seeds); birth-time error.
- Success: DPD keeps MMCS ≥ 0.9 and seed stability ≥ 0.8 in regimes (ratio ≥ 4) where final-checkpoint SPD/VPD drops below 0.7. Ablation: shuffling the checkpoint order must destroy the advantage.

D2. Unsupervised rediscovery of grokking.
- Setup: 1-layer transformer on mod-113 addition (Nanda et al. setup), about 200 checkpoints, with no Fourier prior given to the method.
- Success:
  - Components align with the key Fourier frequencies (cos > 0.8).
  - Memorization components are born early and die during cleanup.
  - Fourier components are born during circuit formation, and their ledger share matches the drop in Nanda's restricted loss.

D3. Real LM, with pre-registered hypotheses.
- Setup: a self-trained 4-layer TinyStories model (5–20M parameters, about 100 log-spaced checkpoints), plus Pythia-14m/70m public revisions.
- H1, developmental reversal: ablating component c in the final model should raise loss on the tokens whose loss fell around c's birth. Success: median per-component Spearman > 0.4, against a random-window null of about 0.
- H2, discreteness: compare a sum-of-sigmoid-births model with a continuous co-growth model on held-out per-token loss curves.
- H3, quanta ordering: Spearman between usage frequency and birth time.
- H4, transients: count components whose g peaks and then falls by more than 50%, and validate each by ablation at the peak checkpoint versus the final one.
- Any outcome is publishable, because each one either supports or falsifies a named theory.
proposals.compute_needs:
- D1 and D2: CPU to one consumer GPU, minutes to hours per run.
- D3 TinyStories 4-layer: training with dense checkpointing takes hours on one GPU; DPD over all matrices takes about 1–3 days on one A100/H100-class GPU, since each step samples one checkpoint and costs roughly one SPD step.
- Pythia-70m: restrict to 2–3 layers to stay on one GPU.
- Storage: 100 checkpoints of a 70M model is about 14 GB in bf16.
- Stage 1 (CP only) is data-free and runs on CPU for small models, so it scales to larger models first.
- Scaling path: decompose layer subsets, use fewer checkpoints concentrated around detected transitions, and warm-start from Stage 1.
proposals.risks:
1. Mechanisms may rotate during formation, which breaks the shared-direction CP assumption. Mitigation: allow penalized drift u_c(t), or fit windowed DPD around births.
2. Temporal collinearity: many mechanisms may grow in lockstep, for example in the early statistical-learning phase, so the time mode adds little information there. Quantify the effective temporal rank and report where identifiability holds.
3. Optimizer and weight-decay artifacts (cf. arXiv 2604.25143). Mitigation: decompose weight states rather than updates, and model a(t)·W(0) explicitly.
4. SPD/VPD hyperparameter sensitivity and cost carry over.
5. Generic CP identifiability is a statement about exact low-rank tensors. Real trajectories have residuals, so the guarantee is a motivation, not a proof. The D1 phase diagram is the real test.
6. Novelty of CP over checkpoints is not fully confirmed: my search budget ran out. Run a literature check first.
7. Real-LM development may turn out to be continuous rather than discrete. That is a negative but important result against the quanta hypothesis, not a failure of the tool.

proposals.title: Developmental Knockout Screen: a CRISPR-style interventional map of which mechanisms are prerequisites, scaffolds, or competitors for others during training
proposals.gap:
Post-hoc interpretability reads only the final weights, so it cannot see scaffolds: mechanisms needed to learn a capability that are absent or inert at the end.
- Evidence that scaffolds exist is scattered and hand-built: strategy coopetition, where in-context learning (ICL) emerges only alongside a slower in-weights strategy (Singh et al. 2025); prev-token → induction dependencies shown with manual activation clamping (Singh et al. 2024; Olsson et al. 2022).
- Data-side interventions (MDA 2026; Patterning 2026) shift the timing of pre-chosen units but do not map dependencies between mechanisms.
- There are competing, untested accounts of how mechanisms assemble: sequential prerequisite chains, versus simultaneous 'nucleation' of all parts (the Kinetics preprint, arXiv 2607.27281), versus independent quanta (Michaud 2023).
- No systematic, unsupervised screen exists that knocks out each discovered mechanism during training and measures the developmental consequences for every other mechanism. Nor has anyone tested whether cheap observational signals predict those consequences.
proposals.idea:
Branch training from checkpoint t_b, just before a target mechanism forms, and run short continuations under weight-space knockouts of one component or cluster c. Units come from Chronoscope (Proposal 1). Standalone fallback: attention heads, OV/QK SVD directions, or final-checkpoint SPD/VPD components.

Intervention operators:
- Gradient knockout: after every AdamW step, including the weight-decay term, project the update off c's subspace: ΔW ← ΔW − P_U ΔW P_V. A stronger variant is ΔW ← (I − P_U) ΔW. This is gradient routing done in parameter subspaces rather than on neurons.
- Clamp: hold g_c(t) at its branch value. This is the weight-space analogue of activation clamping.
- Data knockout: drop the top q% of tokens by projected-gradient alignment ⟨∇L(x), u_c v_c^T⟩.
- Knock-in / transplant: install c's final-checkpoint weights early, to test whether that rescues or accelerates dependents.

Readout: re-fit every library component's growth curve on each branch by cheap projection onto the fixed library, and track per-token loss and capability probes. The interaction matrix D[c→d] is the shift in log birth time and in final magnitude of d, as a z-score against a null of matched-norm, matched-rank random-subspace knockouts.

Edges are classified as:
- Prerequisite: d is delayed or prevented.
- Scaffold: prerequisite, and c is transient or has near-zero final-model ablation effect.
- Competitor: d is accelerated.
- Independent.

The screen also compares this interventional ground truth against cheap observational predictors that could replace it at scale:
- birth-order precedence;
- the Hessian cross-term ∂²L/∂g_c∂g_d at t_b, computed with HVPs;
- susceptibility or loss-kernel cross-covariances restricted to the component subspaces (devinterp);
- virtual-weight connectivity, i.e. c writes into the subspace d reads from.

Ships as `chronoscope.screen`, with a branch scheduler, null controls, and a DAG viewer.
proposals.why_new_understanding:
It turns developmental interpretability from describing what happened into causal experiments on how learning is organized. Questions it answers:
- Do neural networks rely on scaffolds that final-weight interpretability can never see? If they do, auditing finished models is incomplete in principle, and it is a concrete way to prevent capabilities: suppress the scaffold.
- Is mechanism assembly sequential or nucleation-like?
- Is the developmental dependency graph sparse and modular, or dense?
- Can memorization scaffold generalization, or does it only compete with it? This is debated for grokking.

If observational signals turn out to predict the interventional DAG, the field gets a validated, retraining-free developmental causal model that scales to large models.

proposals.risks:
1. Compensation and rerouting: under AdamW, networks may route around a rank-1 knockout (arXiv 2604.25143 found rank-3 subspace removal negligible). Mitigation: knock out whole clusters, measure rerouting explicitly by tracking newly born replacement components, and treat rerouting rate as a finding.
2. Off-manifold artifacts: projection changes optimizer statistics. Mitigation: use matched random-subspace nulls and apply projections after the optimizer step.
3. Dependence on unit quality: this needs reasonable mechanisms. Fallback is heads, SVD directions, or final-checkpoint SPD components.
4. Branch-point choice: too late and dependents already exist; too early and everything is perturbed. Mitigation: use 2–3 branch points around each Chronoscope birth time.
5. Combinatorics: all-pairs screens are infeasible at scale. Mitigation: screen single knockouts and read effects on all other components at once (one branch gives a whole column of D), then prioritize with observational predictors.

proposals.title: The Free-Energy Ledger: a falsifiable, quantitative law for which mechanism forms when, tested by pre-registered interventions on data frequency and mechanism complexity
proposals.gap:
Several frameworks each partly explain when things are learned, and none has been tested at the level of individual mechanisms:
- Singular learning theory's internal model selection: Bayesian free energy ≈ nL + λ·log n. It is validated only for a few competing global solutions, in in-context linear regression and parentheses balancing (Carroll et al. 2025; Hoogland et al. 2024; Patterning 2026).
- The Quantization Model: learning order follows usage frequency.
- Distributional simplicity bias (Belrose et al. 2024).
- Optimization hardness: SGD on sparse parity needs about n^k time (Barak et al. 2022).
- The 2026 'kinetics' rate law, exp(−βK) in the number of missing parts K.

Emergence forecasting so far (arXiv 2609.19000) predicts the timing of one predefined capability from empirical precursors. It does not say why a mechanism appears when it does, and it cannot predict birth order across many mechanisms. Resolution's own papers list 'SGD behaves like the Bayesian posterior' as an unproven assumption. No study measures, for many discovered mechanisms, both the loss benefit (ΔL_c) and the complexity cost (Δλ_c) and then tests a quantitative birth law against interventions.
proposals.idea:
For each mechanism c, measure two quantities.
- ΔL_c, nats per token saved: the population-loss increase when c is ablated, or c's share of the Chronoscope ledger.
- Δλ_c, complexity cost: LLC(full) − LLC(c ablated), and alternatively a weight-restricted LLC along c's parameter subspace. Both are estimated with devinterp's SGLD.

SLT internal model selection predicts that c becomes favored once n_eff(t)·ΔL_c ≥ Δλ_c·log n_eff(t). So predicted birth time t*_c and birth order follow from the price ratio ρ_c = Δλ_c/ΔL_c: cheap, high-value mechanisms come first. The same crossing logic predicts when one mechanism replaces another, which covers transients and memorization-to-generalization handoffs.

n_eff(t), the map from tokens × learning-rate schedule to effective sample size, is calibrated with one scalar per run on training-set mechanisms only. All tests are then out-of-sample, on held-out mechanisms and interventions.

The model is pitted head-to-head against:
- frequency-only (quanta);
- complexity-only (simplicity bias);
- optimization-hardness (n^k);
- the kinetics rate law (missing parts K).

The decisive test is interventional, with predictions written down before training:
- Change the data frequency of a held-out mechanism's triggering contexts by ×{0.25, 0.5, 2, 4}.
- Change its intrinsic complexity: lookup-table size, or parity order k ± 1.
- Predict the full curve of birth-time shifts t*(k) before training, then train and compare.

Ships as `chronoscope.ledger.freeenergy`, with mechanism-zoo task generators, LLC-per-component estimators, and a pre-registration and scoring harness.
proposals.why_new_understanding:
If the law holds, it gives a predictive account at the level of individual mechanisms of why networks learn what they learn when they do. It links interpretability (what the mechanism is) with learning theory (its price and value), and makes patterning-style steering of internal structure quantitatively plannable.

If it fails in a structured way, the pattern says which regime applies. For example, a frequency-only fit plus an n^k dependence on k means optimization hardness rather than Bayesian selection governs SGD at the mechanism level. That directly tests the SGD-as-posterior assumption underlying the whole susceptibility and patterning program.

Either way, the field gets its first mechanism-level, quantitative, interventional test of competing theories of emergence and scaling.

proposals.minimal_demo:
Mechanism zoo 1: multitask sparse parity in the Michaud style, 20–30 subtasks with varied parity order k (complexity) and power-law frequencies (value), on a 2-layer MLP.
Mechanism zoo 2: a 2-layer transformer on a mixture of lookup, bigram, skip-trigram, and induction subtasks with varied table sizes and frequencies.

Protocol:
- Identify each subtask's mechanism, using ground truth or Chronoscope components.
- Estimate ΔL_c and Δλ_c at the final checkpoint and fit n_eff on half of the subtasks.
- Predict birth times for the other half.
- Pre-register predicted t*(k) for 10 held-out subtasks under frequency ×{0.25, 0.5, 2, 4} and complexity ±1, then retrain with 3 seeds each.

Success:
- Spearman ≥ 0.8 between predicted and observed log birth times on held-out interventions.
- The free-energy model cuts log-time MAE by at least 30% against the best single-factor or hardness baseline.
- The predicted functional form of the frequency shift, roughly inverse with a log correction, beats the alternatives on likelihood.

Falsification criteria are fixed in advance: if the frequency-only or n^k models match or beat it, the law fails.

Finally, a correlational check on a 4-layer TinyStories model with Chronoscope components: birth order versus ρ_c.

2. Restricted LLC on a component subspace may not equal the marginal complexity Δλ_c. Compare both estimators.
3. n_eff is a free calibration parameter. Guard against overfitting by strict held-out evaluation and a single scalar per run.
4. Mechanisms interact non-additively, so ΔL and Δλ depend on context. Measure them conditionally on the mechanisms already present at the birth time.
5. The Bayes-versus-SGD gap may dominate (learning-rate schedule, AdamW, weight decay). That is a legitimate scientific outcome, but it limits the practical predictive use.
6. The parity task bakes in optimization hardness, so include lookup and induction tasks, where hardness and free energy make different predictions.

surveys.lens_summary:
STATE OF DICTIONARY LEARNING, OCTOBER 2026

1) The architectures have matured and the main tool has shifted from SAEs toward transcoders.
- Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) moved from L1 to TopK (Gao et al. 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04093), JumpReLU (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14435), BatchTopK (https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06410) and Matryoshka (Bussmann et al. 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.17547).
- Transcoders (Dunefsky et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11944) and skip transcoders now beat SAEs on interpretability (Paulo et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18823).
- Cross-layer transcoders (CLTs) plus attribution graphs (Ameisen et al. 2025, https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/methods.html) are now the main circuit instrument. CLT-Forge (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21014) is an open library for them. Gemma Scope 2 ships SAEs and transcoders for every layer of Gemma 3 (270M–27B), with CLTs for the 270M and 1B models (https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/YQro5LyYjDzZrBCdb/announcing-gemma-scope-2).
- Other variants: crosscoders (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/crosscoders/index.html), MOLT, a sparse mixture of linear transforms (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/bulk-update/index.html), Lorsa for attention (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20938), and Jacobian SAEs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18147).

2) The failure modes are well documented.
- Feature absorption (https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14507) and feature hedging (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11756).
- A wrong L0 (the number of latents active per token) produces wrong features (Chanin & Garriga-Alonso, ICML 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16560).
- Features depend on the random seed: only about 30% are shared across seeds for a 131K-latent SAE on Llama-3-8B (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16615).
- SAEs do not find canonical units; meta-SAEs show latents are compositions of other latents (https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04878).
- SAEs on randomly initialised transformers look about as interpretable as on trained ones (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17727).
- "Dark matter": about half of the SAE error, and over 90% of its norm, can be linearly predicted from the input (https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.14670).
- SAEs trained on synthetic data stay in a "diffuse phase" and never recover the true features (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10299).
- The "Geometric Wall": curvature of the activation manifold predicts each layer's SAE error floor (ICML 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09887).

3) Usefulness has been challenged.
- Google DeepMind deprioritised fundamental SAE research after SAEs lost to linear probes on out-of-distribution harmful-intent detection (https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/4uXCAJNuPKtKBsi28/negative-results-for-saes-on-downstream-tasks). Related evidence comes from sparse-probing work (https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.16681) and AxBench (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17148).
- SAEBench (https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09532) shows that better reconstruction does not translate into better downstream metrics.
- The 'Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability' review (Sharkey et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16496) lists the core problems: linearity and sparsity assumptions, a "bag of features" that ignores geometry, decomposing activations but not mechanisms, attention, and dark matter.
- Apollo Research argues that activation-space methods recover statistics of the data rather than the model's computation (https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/gYfpPbww3wQRaxAFD/activation-space-interpretability-may-be-doomed).

4) The 2025–26 responses fall into four groups.
- (a) Better priors:
  - Manifold-aware dictionaries: Michaud et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02565); Bhalla et al., who describe a "dilution" regime (https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.28119); Subspace-Aware SAEs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06333); bilinear autoencoders (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08891).
  - Temporal priors (Priors in Time, ICLR 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01836).
  - Identifiability (iSAE, ICML 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.31245).
  - The architecture–geometry duality (Hindupur et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01822).
- (b) Moving to parameter space: SPD (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20790) and then VPD. VPD decomposes a 67M-parameter LM including attention and shows no feature splitting (https://static.goodfire.ai/vpd-blog-post/post.md). Weight-sparse training is a related route (https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13653).
- (c) Ground truth: SynthSAEBench uses synthetic activations, not a trained network (https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14687). Board-game models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00113), belief-state HMM transformers (https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15943) and formal languages (https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11767) provide trained-network ground truth.
- (d) Relational structure:
  - SAEs miss entity–attribute bindings that are linearly decodable and causally used, and no fix is offered (Hönig et al., ICML 2026, https://icml.cc/virtual/2026/79592).
  - Tensor-product representation (TPR) structure has been found only with supervision: TPR probes on Othello (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09967) and TPR re-derivations with hand-specified roles (Enyan & McCoy, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29034).

WHAT REMAINS OPEN

Shared diagnosis: every dictionary method still assumes the activation is a bag of independent, identically distributed sparse directions.
- (i) No unsupervised tool recovers continuous variables and the computations between them. Anthropic's own limitations section says multidimensional concepts become "collections of hard-to-distinguish features", supernodes are "a not-very-principled abstraction", and global feature-to-feature weights are "rather difficult to understand". The manifold work of 2026 is single-site and representational only.
- (ii) No unsupervised dictionary exposes binding (which attribute belongs to which entity).
- (iii) There is no network-level ground truth that covers several representation types. So nobody can yet test which ontology is right, what dark matter is, how to pick L0 and width, or whether a feature is more than a null artifact.

The three proposals target (i), (ii) and (iii). Together they aim to replace "bags of directions" with typed variables (continuous, relational, discrete) and the functions between them.

Caveat: the web-search budget ran out near the end of research. A few 2026 preprints were checked only at abstract level (Geometric Wall, Subspace-Aware SAEs, the diffuse-phase paper, the HRR paper).

proposals.title: Atlas Transcoders and Variable Graphs: finding the continuous variables a network computes with, and the functions between them
proposals.gap:
Attribution graphs are the field's main circuit instrument, and they break continuous quantities into many discrete features.
- Anthropic's circuit-tracing limitations section says multidimensional concepts may appear as "collections of hard-to-distinguish features". It calls supernodes "a not-very-principled abstraction to ad-hoc group together related features" and says "global feature-feature connections" are "rather difficult to understand" (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/methods.html).
- When Anthropic did find a geometric algorithm (line-break counting, Gurnee et al. 2025, https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/linebreaks/index.html), it was assembled by hand from "sparse feature families" on one task.
- Number helices (Kantamneni & Tegmark, https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00873) and calendar circles (Engels et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14860) were found with hypotheses specified in advance or with post-hoc clustering.
- The 2026 manifold-aware dictionaries are all single-site and representational: Bhalla et al.'s dilution theory with post-hoc grouping (https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.28119), Subspace-Aware SAEs with linear decoder subspaces (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06333), and bilinear autoencoders (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08891). The bilinear-autoencoder paper explicitly leaves causal ablation and manifold steering to future work and does not analyse computation across layers.
- No method outputs a manifold coordinate together with the function mapping one layer's coordinate to the next. Searches for manifold or continuous-variable transcoders and manifold-level attribution graphs found nothing.
proposals.why_new_understanding:
It changes the unit of a circuit from a bag of discretised features to a small graph of named continuous variables joined by explicit functions. That is the level at which algorithms such as clock arithmetic, counting, dates, positions and magnitudes actually operate.

What it would answer:
- How much of a network's computation is geometric (low-dimensional and continuous), and how much is discrete lookup.
- Which variables recur across layers and models.
- Whether feature splitting is mostly an artifact of discretising manifolds. Michaud et al. predict SAEs waste latents tiling manifolds, and the Geometric Wall ties SAE error floors to curvature. Atlas atoms should absorb those families and lower the floor.

It would also give the first automatic, input-independent circuit descriptions that can be checked by intervention: a coordinate predicts the model's output under counterfactual settings. This is the global-circuits capability Anthropic names as missing.

proposals.minimal_demo:
Stage A: ground truth, CPU only.
- Train the 1-layer transformer grokked on (a+b) mod 113 (Nanda et al. 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.05217). Its known algorithm puts a and b on circles at about 5 key frequencies, and the MLP composes them into cos and sin of w(a+b).
- Also train a 2-layer "calendar" model on weekday and month offset arithmetic written in words.
- Fit an atlas transcoder to the MLP. Pass criteria:
  1. The number of torus→circle atoms equals the number of key frequencies, within ±1.
  2. Circular correlation between each atom's coordinates and w_k·a, w_k·b is above 0.95.
  3. The extracted edge function fits θ_out = θ_a + θ_b with R² above 0.95.
  4. At matched downstream cross-entropy, it uses at least 10× fewer bits per token than a TopK transcoder.
  5. At least 80% of the TopK latents in each frequency family lie on that atom's decoder curve (cosine above 0.9).

Stage B: real LMs, one GPU.
- Models: GPT-2 small, Pythia-410m/1.4b, and Gemma-3-1B. The Gemma Scope 2 CLT for Gemma-3-1B can serve as the initialisation for conversion.
- Tasks: weekday and month arithmetic, multi-digit number addition (helix), and character-count / line-position prompts.
- Metrics:
  - (a) Pareto curves of downstream KL against bits per token, versus TopK, BatchTopK and Matryoshka transcoders, a subspace-SAE baseline and a bilinear autoencoder.
  - (b) Coordinate-steering accuracy on held-out prompts. Set the weekday atom's angle to a target and record the share of top-1 next tokens matching the predicted day. The target is at least 80%, beating the best single-SAE-latent steering and approaching a supervised distributed alignment search (DAS) subspace (upper bound).
  - (c) Composition test. On 2-hop prompts such as "three days after the day before Friday", the composed edge functions must predict the model's outputs under joint coordinate interventions.
  - (d) Discovery sweep over GPT-2 MLP layers 3–9: report all atoms with d ≥ 1, the share of the bits saved over the SAE that comes from chart atoms, and whether the fitted width-scaling error floor drops below the TopK floor.

The idea fails if any of these happen: charts do not beat SAEs at matched bits on real LMs; coordinate steering is no better than SAE latents; or the edge functions are not low-complexity.
proposals.compute_needs:
- Stage A: CPU, minutes to hours. The grokking model trains in under an hour on CPU.
- Stage B: one 24–80 GB GPU.
  - Activations for 100–300M tokens per site for GPT-2 small, Pythia-410m and Gemma-3-1B, cached in fp16 (or streamed).
  - Each atlas atom with M = 16–32 basis functions costs about M×d parameters, so K = 8k atoms × 32 × 768 is about 200M parameters for one GPT-2 layer. Mitigate with low-rank V and by promoting only 5–10% of atoms.
  - Roughly 2–6 GPU-hours per layer for GPT-2, and about 1 GPU-day for a few Gemma-3-1B layers.
  - Variable-graph extraction is cheap: forward passes along decoder curves.
- Builds on interp-lab's SAE and transcoder training for the baselines and the initialisation.
proposals.risks:
- Optimising chart encoders (atan2, chart boundaries) is non-convex. The fit may collapse to linear subspaces, which reduces it to Subspace-Aware SAEs. Mitigations: promote-and-merge initialisation from SAE families, and annealing the chart type.
- Real LLM manifolds may be ragged, higher-dimensional or heavily diluted. Bhalla et al. report diluted manifolds, and bilinear-AE quadratic latents tend to be high-rank, so clean low-dimensional charts may cover only a small fraction of variance. That fraction would itself be a reportable measurement.
- Many geometric transforms are done by attention (in the counting work, heads 'twist' the manifold). Version 1 freezes attention patterns, which gives local rather than global edges for cross-position steps. Version 2 needs QK-aware atoms, possibly via Lorsa or VPD-style attention components.
- MDL precision choices affect type selection, so curves should be reported against precision.
- A weekday or helix demo might be read as cherry-picked. The unsupervised discovery sweep and the bits-saved census guard against this.

proposals.title: Binding Autoencoders: unsupervised discovery of role–filler (tensor-product) structure that SAEs cannot see
proposals.gap:
A sparse code is a bag of features: it can say 'red', 'square', 'blue' and 'circle' are present but not which colour goes with which shape. Models clearly represent that binding.
- Binding-ID vectors (Feng & Steinhardt 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.17191).
- Positional, lexical and reflexive binding mechanisms across nine models (Gur-Arieh, Geva & Geiger, ICLR 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06182).
- Hönig et al. (ICML 2026, https://icml.cc/virtual/2026/79592) build a transformer whose entity–relation address is linearly decodable with full accuracy and causally used. SAEs reconstruct it but do not expose it as clean features, and the paper proposes no fix.
- Every positive tensor-product (TPR) result needs supervision: TPR probes on Othello (Lee, Viégas & Wattenberg 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09967); Enyan & McCoy 2026 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29034), who build a TPR-derived SAE analytically from hand-specified roles on fixed templates and list unsupervised role discovery as a limitation; and TPDNs (McCoy et al. 2019, https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.08718).
- Kim & Dieng (NeurIPS 2026, https://neurips.cc/virtual/2026/157272) use SAE features as a vocabulary for HRR binding but do not discover the model's own binding.
- KronSAE (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22255) adds a compositional co-activation prior but has no notion of roles.
- Wattenberg & Viégas (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14662) call for exactly this tool and warn that relational mechanisms create 'echo' features that confuse SAEs.
proposals.why_new_understanding:
It would be the first unsupervised instrument for relational structure inside networks. It would make visible the pointers, variable bindings and structured world state behind in-context reasoning, entity tracking, belief tracking and multi-hop retrieval, all of which are currently invisible to dictionary methods.

What it would test:
- Whether many SAE 'composite' latents (meta-SAE compositions, echo features, feature splitting along entity × attribute) are really bound pairs.
- Whether bindings account for part of the linearly predictable dark matter. Role × filler combinatorics would leave an SAE with too few atoms, giving structured residuals.
- Whether role space is itself continuous: Feng & Steinhardt found binding IDs form a continuous subspace, and Gur-Arieh et al. found positional binding becomes noisy in middle positions.

It turns 'what does the model represent' into 'what structure does it represent', which is the step from features to representations that compose.

proposals.compute_needs:
- Stages A and B: CPU or one small GPU, a few hours each. OthelloGPT has about 25M parameters and synthetic games are unlimited.
- Stage C: one 24–48 GB GPU.
  - Cache 50–200M tokens of activations for 2–4 layers of Pythia-1.4b or Gemma-2-2b.
  - Encoder cost per token is about O(R·d·q). With R = 64 and q = 128 this is comparable to a 16k-latent SAE.
  - Total roughly 1–2 GPU-days including baselines and causal swap evaluations.
proposals.risks:
- Identifiability: bilinear factorisations have gauge freedom, and roles can absorb filler variance. Gauge-fixing and swap-based causal validation are mandatory, and the stage-A and stage-B ground truth checks this.
- Inferring which role binds which filler is combinatorial. Amortised unbinding may fail with many entities in superposition; a fallback is a few iterative explain-away steps.
- LLMs may implement much of binding through attention pointers resolved at retrieval time (lexical and reflexive mechanisms) rather than through TPR-like states in the residual stream. If so, the BAE would find little binding structure in the residual stream at many sites. That is a valuable negative result, and it points to extending the method to attention components.
- Bilinear capacity can soak up generic variance and look good on reconstruction, so every comparison must be at matched description length and include held-out swap tests.

proposals.title: The Representation Census: typed, complete decompositions checked against known-world model organisms (settling what dark matter is, and which ontology is right)
proposals.gap:
The field cannot currently test its central assumption, that representations are sparse linear features, against alternatives, because it has no ground truth for trained networks covering several representation types.
- SynthSAEBench (Chanin & Garriga-Alonso 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14687) generates synthetic activations with no network computation.
- Other ground-truth setups cover one representation type each: board games give board state only (https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00113); formal languages give grammar variables (Menon et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11767); belief-state HMM transformers show simplex geometry but were studied by regression, not decomposition (Shai et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15943; Piotrowski et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01954). Levinson's 2026 pipeline (https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.02685) is a single, preliminary study.
- Dark matter is unexplained (Engels et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.14670; Anthropic's CLT limitations). The Geometric Wall attributes error floors to curvature (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09887). Trained SAEs on synthetic data stay in a diffuse, non-recovering phase (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10299).
- L0 and width are unprincipled and change which features appear: wrong-L0 results (https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16560) and hedging (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11756).
- No pipeline calibrates against nulls: random-init networks look interpretable (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17727) and features vary across seeds (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16615).
- Searches found no study that splits LM activation variance between sparse, manifold, relational and dense structure.
proposals.why_new_understanding:
It would give the first quantitative, falsifiable answer to whether networks represent the world as sparse linear features, and if not, what fraction is manifold, relational, belief-simplex or dense, layer by layer and across scale.

- It would turn dark matter from a nuisance into a measured breakdown. It would test whether the SAE error floor (Geometric Wall) is broken by typed atoms at equal bits.
- It would replace L0 and width tuning with a selection criterion validated against ground truth.
- It would answer the random-network and seed-instability critiques directly with null-calibrated, consensus structure.
- Either outcome is a landmark. If nearly everything is assigned to point atoms, the linear-sparse ontology is vindicated with ground-truth backing. If not, the field gets a map of what SAEs are structurally blind to.
- The organism suite becomes the referee for every future dictionary method, including SAE variants, transcoders, iSAE, Subspace-Aware SAEs, bilinear autoencoders and VPD.
