proposals.minimal_demo:
Models:
- Train 1-layer and 2-layer transformers (d=256, 8 heads, 4x MLP, 4096-token BPE) on TinyStories or SimpleStories (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.09184), saving about 50 checkpoints each. Also train attention-only variants.
- Calibration model: the same architecture trained on a synthetic language whose probabilistic generator program is known.
- Sanity checks: two or three Huang et al. algorithmic tasks, where the known programs must be recovered.

Metrics, on 1M held-out tokens:
- Explained fraction EF = 1 − KL(M‖P)/KL(M‖unigram).
- L(P) in bits: the arithmetic-coded source plus tables.
- S(P) compared with L(M), the weights at 4 bits.
- Module interchange-alignment score.
- Error agreement: on tokens where M's top-1 prediction is wrong, P makes the same mistake. This is compared with an N-gram rule-set baseline of matched size (Nguyen 2024) and with pruning-only and heads-only (Hayes-style) baselines.

Success:
- 1-layer model: a weight-free program with EF ≥ 0.85, L(P) ≤ 10% of L(M), alignment ≥ 0.9, and error agreement significantly above the matched-bits N-gram baseline.
- 2-layer model: EF ≥ 0.7.
- Synthetic-language model: recover ≥ 4 of the 5 generator rules the model learned.
- Developmental run: at least one discrete program commit coincides with the induction-head loss bump.

Falsification: if EF saturates below 0.5 before L(P) reaches L(M), that is a quantified upper bound on how programmable LMs are at this scale. This is still a first-of-its-kind result.
proposals.compute_needs:
One modest GPU. A 1-layer attention-only model is CPU-feasible.
- Training each small model: about 1–3 GPU-hours.
- Candidate evaluation is cheap because 1-layer and 2-layer logits decompose additively over cached activations. Expect 10^4–10^5 rewrites per model, at seconds to minutes each.
- LLM API for rule proposals and naming: roughly 5k–20k calls (about $100–800). A local 7–8B code model is a cheaper option at lower quality.
- Total: about 20–60 GPU-hours for the 1-layer and 2-layer models, the calibration model, and the developmental series.
proposals.risks:
- MLP knowledge may be irreducibly table-like, so EF plateaus. The honest bit ledger makes this a reportable result rather than a failure.
- Nonlinearities in LayerNorm, softmax and GELU cause errors to compound when modules are substituted. Mitigations: LN-free fine-tuning and calibrated soft surrogates.
- The search may find compact but unreadable numerical kernels. Programs must be written in named DSL primitives with LLM docstrings, plus human spot checks of a random sample of modules.
- KL may be dominated by the long tail of rare tokens. Report breakdowns by token type.
- LLM-proposed rules may encode knowledge of the data rather than the model's mechanism. The alignment certificate and the error-agreement test guard against this.
- Composition across layers (virtual heads) can blow up the size of the 2-layer IR. Prioritize by effectiveness and charge for cross terms.

proposals.title: POPPER: adversarial explainer–falsifier self-play over executable mechanistic simulators, scored by held-out intervention prediction
proposals.gap:
Current interpretability outputs do not measurably improve prediction:
- CHIVE (Anthropic, Aug 2026): activation oracles, NLAs and SAEs gave no uplift over transcript-only predictors of counterfactual behaviour.
- Pando (Apr 2026): SAEs and circuit tracing gave no reliable benefit.
- Published circuits (IOI, docstring) diverge from the full model on ordinary inputs under adversarial search (uit de Bos & Garriga-Alonso 2024).
- Faithfulness scores swing with the choice of ablation (Miller et al. 2024).
- Pruned circuits can be interpretable yet unfaithful (Drori 2026).

Agentic interpreters exist: MAIA, InterpAgent (May 2026), HyVE (Jun 2026) and SAEScientist-Bench (Sep 2026). All report that validation is the bottleneck and that agents misread measurements, because there is no automatic arbiter that resists gaming. ObserverBench (Sep 2026) predicts held-out ablation effects with ridge regressors, not with explanations.

No method yet requires an explanation to predict the model's behaviour under internal interventions it never saw, while an adversary searches for counterexamples.
proposals.idea:
(1) Shared component registry and typed intervention algebra.
- Components: heads, MLP neurons, transcoder/SAE latents, SPD/VPD subcomponents, residual directions.
- Operations: resample or mean ablation, sender→receiver path patching, norm-bounded steering, input edits.
- All are kept on-manifold, and several ablation semantics are pre-registered.

(2) Explanations are executable Mechanistic Simulators. A simulator is short, length-capped, MDL-charged Python that takes (prompt, intervention set), returns the predicted output distribution or logit difference, and must refer to components by their registry names.

(3) Explainer agent. An LLM with tools writes and revises simulators. Tools: activation reading, circuit-tracer attribution graphs, SAE features, and interp-lab's evidence grading and InterventionRunner.

(4) Falsifier, two kinds:
- (a) Gradient-based search over relaxed masks, patch interpolations and input embeddings to maximize simulator error, similar to VPD's adversarial masks.
- (b) An LLM agent that proposes semantic counterexamples.
Counterexamples go back to the explainer, which closes the self-play loop.

(5) Arbiter. A pre-registered, procedurally generated held-out intervention distribution, split by intervention type. Explanations are built from single-component evidence and then tested on multi-component ablations, path patches and steering. Generalizing compositionally to unseen intervention types is the operational definition of mechanistic understanding as opposed to curve-fitting. A leaderboard ranks explanations ('Elo for explanations') at a fixed falsifier budget.

Synergy: a DECOMPILE program is itself a simulator, so POPPER can stress-test it directly.
proposals.why_new_understanding:
Interpretability claims become predictions with a proper scoring rule. That makes it possible, for the first time, to measure whether an explanation contains information about the internals that a black-box regressor given the same data lacks. This is the mechanistic counterpart to CHIVE's negative result, and it can be falsified either way.

On canonical circuits, POPPER will show exactly which interactions the human stories leave out: backup and negative heads, Hydra-style self-repair, nonlinear compositions. It will then produce complete simulators that include them.

Self-play gives automated interpretability a non-gameable training signal. That is a path to microscopes that improve through search and compute rather than human effort, and it carries over to any model with a component registry.

proposals.minimal_demo:
Targets:
- GPT-2 small on IOI (https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.00593) and greater-than (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.00586).
- Pythia-160m on induction.
- 4–8 InterpBench models with planted circuits as ground truth (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14494).

Baselines:
- (i) The published circuit turned into a simulator: a forward pass through the circuit only, plus an LLM translation of the paper's claims.
- (ii) An ObserverBench-style ridge or pairwise regressor trained on the same number of interventions.
- (iii) A transcript-only LLM predictor.
- (iv) ACDC (https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14997) or EAP circuits.

Metrics:
- R² or KL of predicted vs actual outputs on held-out intervention types.
- Worst-case error at a fixed falsifier budget.
- Number of interventions consumed.

Success:
- On IOI, POPPER simulators reach R² ≥ 0.8 on held-out multi-head ablations and path patches, where the published-circuit and additive/ridge baselines reach ≤ 0.5. They should do this with at least 10 times fewer interventions than the regressor.
- On InterpBench, recover the planted circuits with ≥ 90% edge precision.
- Falsifier worst-case error falls monotonically across rounds.
- Backup and negative name-mover structure is rediscovered without supervision.

Falsification: if simulators never beat a regressor with matched data on unseen intervention types, mechanistic explanations confer no predictive advantage. That would be a major negative result.
proposals.compute_needs:
- GPT-2 small and Pythia-160m interventions: about 10^5–10^6 short-prompt forward passes, roughly 2–10 GPU-hours. This is CPU-feasible with batching but slower.
- The gradient falsifier is cheap: backprop through masks.
- LLM agent API for explainer and semantic falsifier: about $500–3k across all runs. There is a tradeoff between capping agent rounds and simulator quality.
proposals.risks:
- Simulators may degenerate into regressors with component names attached. Mitigations: length cap, MDL charge, and evaluation split by intervention type.
- The falsifier may exploit off-manifold interventions. Restrict to resample and mean ablation and to norm-bounded steering.
- Results can still depend on ablation semantics. Pre-register several and report all of them.
- Agent cost and variance between runs.
- It partly overlaps interp-lab's causal grading. Position interp-lab as the evidence and intervention layer that POPPER builds on, not something POPPER duplicates.
- Wins on well-studied circuits may not carry over to open-ended behaviours.

proposals.title: WEIGHTREADER: an amortized decompiler that reads SGD-trained transformer weights and writes the program they actually run (with population-scale 'ecology of algorithms')
proposals.gap:
Existing decompilation falls into two kinds, neither of which reads naturally trained weights:
- Per-model search: MIPS, and D-RASP (Huang et al. 2026), which needs staged pruning and primitive matching for each model and only works on length-generalizing models.
- Learned, but on weights produced by a compiler: Thurnherr & Riesen 2024 get 30% exact and more than 70% functionally equivalent programs, on Tracr only; also Langosco et al.'s meta-models.

Related work does not close the gap. Weight-space learning (model zoos, equivariant neural functional networks) predicts coarse properties. DIT (Goel et al. 2025) verbalizes simple fine-tuning diffs. Pando (2026) builds zoos for evaluation, not for decompilation.

No model reads SGD-trained weights and outputs the mechanism rather than the task. Whether a network's choice of algorithm can be read from its weights at population scale has never been tested. For example, Clock vs Pizza on modular addition (Zhong et al. 2023) is still diagnosed by hand, one model at a time. Even ARC's 432-parameter AlgZoo RNN is unexplained.
proposals.idea:
(1) Procedural task generator. Sample programs from a RASP-like DSL: select, aggregate and map, depth ≤ 3. The families include the Huang et al. tasks, Dyck languages, counting, sorting variants and modular arithmetic. Deliberately leave freedom in the training distribution so that several algorithms fit the data.

(2) A zoo of about 10^5 tiny transformers: 1–2 layers, d=32–64, 1–4 heads, LayerNorm on or off, with varied learning rate, weight decay and seed. Train them in batches with torch.func.vmap on one GPU and save checkpoints.

(3) Symmetry-canonical weight encoding.
- Represent each head by basis-free virtual matrices in token and position space (E·W_QK·Eᵀ, P·W_QK·Pᵀ, and OV projected through W_U).
- Represent each MLP neuron by its token-space input and output vectors.
- Encode them with a set-transformer over heads and neurons.
This removes the residual-rotation and permutation symmetries that defeat naive weight readers.

(4) A decoder that emits a DSL program, trained in two stages:
- (a) Supervised on task programs, plus per-model mechanism labels from running a D-RASP-style decompiler on a subset as teacher, plus Tracr warm-start pairs.
- (b) RL against an execution verifier. The reward is agreement between the program's execution and the network's outputs on probe inputs, including OOD lengths and adversarial edge cases. The reader therefore learns to transcribe the algorithm the network actually runs, bugs included, rather than the intended task.

(5) Population science. Label every model in the zoo and map which algorithm SGD selects as a function of hyperparameters, data and width. Confirm the claims with targeted mechanistic tests on sampled models.
proposals.why_new_understanding:
If mechanisms can be decoded from weights in one forward pass, interpretability becomes a learned perception problem, with measurable error rates. The analogy is AlphaFold for structure, here weights → program.

- Population-scale readouts allow statistical laws of algorithm selection that one-at-a-time analysis cannot reach. Examples: the Clock/Pizza phase diagram, how often length-generalizing programs arise, which training choices yield 'buggy' algorithms.
- The test of predicting the network's own idiosyncratic failures from its weights measures mechanistic content directly, over and above knowing the task.
- Head-level transfer to GPT-2 small and Pythia tests whether a universal vocabulary of weight motifs exists across scales.

proposals.minimal_demo:
Setup: a zoo of 20k–100k models over about 150 DSL programs. Hold out 30 programs, including novel compositions, and 2 architecture settings.

Tests:
- (a) Functional equivalence of the decoded program to the network itself, defined as ≥ 95% agreement on a probe set, on held-out programs. Target ≥ 60%, against < 10% for the nearest-neighbour-in-weight-space and task-classifier baselines.
- (b) Failure prediction from weights alone. Target AUROC ≥ 0.8 for predicting which OOD inputs a held-out network gets wrong (the task-only baseline is about 0.5), and ≥ 50% exact prediction of the wrong output.
- (c) Clock vs Pizza identification on modular-addition models: ≥ 95% accuracy against Zhong et al.'s diagnostics (gradient symmetricity, distance irrelevance), plus a phase diagram over width, weight decay and attention rate.
- (d) Agreement with D-RASP search on Huang et al.'s models at ≥ 100 times lower wall-clock time.
- (e) Stretch: zero-shot head-type labels on GPT-2 small (previous-token, induction, duplicate-token, name-mover), compared with labels from the literature.

Falsification: if the reader only matches the task-classifier baseline on (b) and (c), the mechanism is not learnable from weights this way at this scale.
proposals.compute_needs:
- Zoo models have about 5k–50k parameters. With vmap at about 1000 models per batch, 10^5 models take roughly 5–30 GPU-hours on a modest GPU.
- CPU-only: about 10^4 models in a day.
- Reader: a 20–50M-parameter transformer, about 5–20 GPU-hours including RL with a fast Python/NumPy DSL executor.
- Teacher decompilation on about 2k models: parallel on CPU.
- No LLM API is needed for the core result. One is optional for naming discovered program families.
proposals.risks:
- The reader may learn task identity rather than mechanism. The failure-prediction and ambiguous-algorithm tests are designed to catch this.
- DSL coverage limits what can be expressed. Mitigation: an escape hatch that allows lookup tables, charged by MDL.
- The distribution shift to natural LMs is large, so claims about scaling stay conjectural until the head-level transfer (e) works.
- The RL stage could be reward-hacked by degenerate programs. Mitigations: MDL penalty and held-out probes.
- Labels from the teacher decompiler are noisy and biased toward length-generalizing models.
